newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Israeli leader offers to help Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Israeli leader offers to help Netanyahu.

text.p: Former Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres offered parliamentary backing on Monday for his successor, Benjamin Netanyahu, if any peace moves Netanyahu makes result in the breaking up of his coalition government.

Speaking to U.S. Jewish leaders, Peres defended his efforts for peace that ended with his defeat in last May's elections and made oblique references to right-wing criticism of Netanyahu for finally meeting Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and shaking his hand last week.
"Better later than never," Peres said of the handshake. "Once you have shaken a hand, you have a shaken position."
Several right-wing leaders crticized Netanyahu's meeting with Arafat and the prime minister threatened to dismiss any minister who did not support him.

But Peres said, "If the government does not have a majority in parliament, we will support it." Asked later if he would consider entering into a national unity government, he shook his head and said, "I am not the one to propose a national unity government. It is not my desire to be a member of such a government."

He said the Netanyahu government must be judged on what it does rather than on what it says. And he accused it of refusing to make the compromises needed for peace with Syria, warning that time was not on Israel's side.

"The Jewish people do not have enough time as we may think," Peres said of forces in the Middle East that could interfere in the peace process -- including the dangers of terrorism, the spread of non-conventional weapons and the rise of Islamic fundamentalism.

Peres warned Netanyahu, who does not want to give up any part of the Golan Heights, that peace would not come without a price -- especially with Syria. "We can't have peace without a price. There can be no peace with Syria without a compromise on the Golan Heights. It is my deep conviction. (But) I do not see such a peace in the future."

Spelling out yet another another difference between his government and Netanyahu's, he said, "We look at (Palestinian) autonomy as a stage on the road to a permanent solution, not as the permanent solution." He urged Netanyahu to fulfil the agreements the Peres government made on self-rule for Hebron.
Peres praised U.S. President Bill Clinton for his strong reaction to last week's move by Iraqi forces into Kurdish areas in the north of Iraq.

He said Middle Eastern criticism of the U.S. missile attacks were based on a fear that Iraq could be destroyed by internal strife. But he said the real danger was Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein, who if left to his own devices could have an atomic weapon developed with "a year's time."
